Parse a Vector of Names

Source: R/parse_all_names.R
parse_names.Rd

Parses a character vector of raw names into a data frame of structured name components. Names are sanitized once up front and then parsed with parse_name().

Usage

parse_names(
  x,
  prefixes = prx,
  suffixes = sfx,
  split_initials = FALSE,
  add_nicknames = FALSE,
  split_run_together = FALSE,
  classify = FALSE,
  workers = NULL,
  ...
)

Arguments

x

A character vector of raw names to parse.

prefixes

A character vector of salutations/prefixes to remove. Defaults to prx.

suffixes

A character vector of suffixes to remove. Defaults to sfx.

split_initials

Logical; forwarded to parse_name() to enable the opt-in Defect 3 stray-initial split. Defaults to FALSE.

add_nicknames

Logical; if TRUE, append the nickname columns from nickname_lookup() (first_name_type, first_name_formal, first_name_nicknames, first_name_canonical, canonical_rule). Defaults to FALSE.

split_run_together

Logical; if TRUE, split a surname and given name written as one word (KramerKenneth, MURPHYSANDRA) before parsing, with split_run_together(). Defaults to FALSE.

classify

Logical; if TRUE, add the name_type and org_score columns from classify_names(), computed on the raw input, so that organisations, placeholders and couples can be set aside. Defaults to FALSE.

workers

NULL (default) to use the caller's future::plan() (sequential unless the caller set one), 1 to run in this session whatever the plan, or a number above 1 to start that many workers for this call. See Parallel parsing.

...

Reserved for future arguments; currently unused.

Value

A data.frame with one row per input name and columns name (the original input) plus the parsed components returned by parse_name(): salutation, first_name, middle_name, last_name, suffix, status, gender, and gender_confidence, plus the nickname columns when add_nicknames = TRUE and name_type and org_score when classify = TRUE.

Parallel parsing

By default parse_names() runs in the current R session and never starts background processes on its own. It uses parallel workers in two cases:

  • the caller has set a future::plan(), for example future::plan(future::multisession, workers = 4). The workers are reused across calls until the caller changes the plan;

  • workers is a number above 1. parse_names() starts that many background R sessions for this call and shuts them down when it returns, restoring the caller's plan.

Workers load the installed copy of peopleparser. Each one reports its version and build time, and parse_names() stops if any differs from the calling session (for example after a reinstall while R was running, or when the session runs development code through devtools::load_all()). Starting workers takes a few seconds, so they pay off only for large inputs.

Examples

x <- c("livingston III,  Mr. MICHAEL JOHN9", "THOMAS H VON KAMECKE")
parse_names(x)
#>                                 name salutation first_name middle_name
#> 1 livingston III,  Mr. MICHAEL JOHN9         MR    MICHAEL        JOHN
#> 2               THOMAS H VON KAMECKE                THOMAS           H
#>     last_name suffix status gender gender_confidence
#> 1  LIVINGSTON    III             M              99.8
#> 2 VON-KAMECKE                    M              99.9

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
# start 4 workers for one large call
parse_names(big_vector, workers = 4)

# or keep workers running across several calls
future::plan(future::multisession, workers = 4)
a <- parse_names(batch_1)
b <- parse_names(batch_2)
future::plan(future::sequential)
} # }
